en.title: Reading a program
en.story: A program contains both message text and instructions about that text. Read this working example and separate those two roles. Tray ready is the message; the output operation and surrounding punctuation tell the language what to do with it. Predict what appears before running. You do not need to name every symbol to make a useful prediction. Start by finding the matching quote marks and reading the characters between them. Compare the result with that message, including its space and capitalization.
en.idea: Changing message characters and changing code punctuation have different consequences. Replacing ready with waiting gives the same output operation a different string. Removing the closing quote breaks the string's boundary, so the runtime or compiler may report an error instead of producing the intended message. Error wording differs between tracks and versions. Read the first reported source location, compare it with the working example, and repair one small difference. A highlighted line is a useful starting point, but the missing symbol may belong just before that location.
en.make: Change the sign to Tray waiting and check it. Then, if you want to investigate an error, remove a closing quote in your editable program and check again. Observe the first diagnostic before restoring the quote. This is a reversible experiment, not a test of how many mistakes you can avoid. The repair exercise below keeps the output operation intact and asks you to inspect the message. Distinguish a program that runs with the wrong text from a program that cannot run at all.
en.recap: Read a string's boundaries before editing its contents. A wrong message can produce valid but incorrect output; broken source punctuation can prevent the intended program from running. Neither result says anything about your ability to learn. Use the evidence to choose the next action: compare output characters for a message mismatch, or inspect the first diagnostic for a source error. Recall this distinction before revealing the cards. In the next lesson, the program receives text from input so its message can change without editing the source each time.
